extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, journalists, and legal researchers interested in U.S. obscenity law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal tests, statutory rules, and doctrinal distinctions used in the United States to determine when sexual or related material is legally obscene or may be regulated (including broadcast/child-pornography exceptions and state device bans). Useful for understanding how courts and regulators evaluate allegedly obscene material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miller test (three-pronged obscenity test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic guidelines for the trier of fact must be: (a) whether 'the average person, applying contemporary community standards' would find that the work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest; (b) whether the work depicts or describes, in a patently offensive way, sexual conduct specifically defined by the applicable state law; and (c) whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Miller test remains U.S. judicial precedent for determining obscenity. Key points: apply 'contemporary community standards'; evaluate the work 'taken as a whole'; the second prong requires sexual conduct be 'specifically defined' by state law; only the first two prongs are treated as factual questions for a jury applying community standards, while the third prong (serious value) is judged by whether a reasonable person would find such value. Examples and applications in the article include film and print cases; the test can produce different results in different jurisdictions and has important consequences for internet-distributed material.

rubrics_metrics.name: First prong: appeals to the prurient interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether, to the average person applying contemporary community standards, the dominant theme of the material, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'prurient interest' element used in Roth and retained in Miller. 'Taken as a whole' means isolated passages cannot by themselves make a work obscene. The 'average person' and 'community standards' language ties the inquiry to local norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second prong: patent offensiveness with specificity by law
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work depicts or describes, in a patently offensive way, sexual conduct specifically defined by the applicable state law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that the allegedly offensive sexual conduct be defined by statute; 'patently offensive' is measured against community standards for that medium. The requirement for statutory specificity limits vagueness challenges to some degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third prong: lack of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value (reasonable person standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court clarified that evaluation of serious value is not measured by an ordinary community member but by whether a reasonable person would find such value (Pope v. Illinois). This prong protects works with bona fide value even if the first two prongs might be met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roth obscenity standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to the average person, applying contemporary community standards, the dominant theme of the material, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Roth test (Roth v. United States, 1957) replaced the older Hicklin approach and formed the foundation for later obscenity jurisprudence; it focuses on dominant theme and prurient interest. It was later refined and folded into Miller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hicklin test (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined material as obscene if it tended 'to deprave or corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences, and into whose hands a publication of this sort may fall.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nineteenth-century test (from Regina v. Hicklin) used in early U.S. cases; considered overbroad because it considered isolated passages and the most susceptible persons. It has been superseded by Roth and Miller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wepplo test (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: If material has a substantial tendency to deprave or corrupt its readers by inciting lascivious thoughts or arousing lustful desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state-court-derived standard (People v. Wepplo, 1947) once used by some courts but invalidated/superseded by later federal standards such as Roth and Miller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast obscenity/indecency standards (FCC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under FCC rules and federal law, radio stations and over-the-air television channels cannot air obscene material at any time and cannot air indecent material between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indecent material is defined as language or pictures that, in context, describe or depict, in terms patently offensive as measured by contemporary community standards for the broadcast medium, sexual or excretory organs or activities. The Supreme Court's Pacifica decision (the 'seven dirty words' case) is central to broadcast regulation. Cable and satellite are treated differently from over-the-air broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child pornography exception (New York v. Ferber and Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Child pornography produced with actual minors is unprotected by the First Amendment even when it is not obscene; child pornography that is produced without using an actual minor (computer-generated images) may be protected if it is not found to be obscene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York v. Ferber holds real-child pornography may be banned regardless of Miller; Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition held that virtual child pornography can be protected speech absent obscenity. The article emphasizes that child pornography is treated as a record of child sexual abuse and attracts severe criminal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community standards and jurisdictional application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Miller test's reliance on 'contemporary community standards' means that the same material can be obscene in one jurisdiction but protected in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet distribution complicates the community-standards approach because material accessible everywhere may be judged by the most restrictive community (e.g., United States v. Thomas). Jurisdictional limits (federal vs state) also affect enforcement: federal statutes apply to interstate or foreign commerce and the U.S. mail; intrastate matters often fall to state law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory prohibitions on distribution and transportation (Title 18, Chapter 71)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several sections of 18 U.S. Code, Chapter 71, prohibit the transmission of obscenity — e.g., transportation of obscene matters for sale or distribution is criminal under 18 U.S.C. § 1465.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal obscenity laws apply to distribution in interstate or foreign commerce and through the U.S. mail. U.S. Customs generally prohibit entry of obscene articles. Prosecution may be pursued under these statutes when distribution crosses state or national lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession vs. distribution (Stanley v. Georgia and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that state laws making mere private possession of obscene material a crime are invalid, at least absent an intent to sell, expose, or circulate the material; however, there is no constitutional right to possess child pornography or to provide obscene material for private use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes private possession from commercial distribution; possession protections are limited (child pornography excluded) and do not create a right to distribute or to acquire for private use from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscene devices / sex toy regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states have prohibited the sale of sexual devices on the ground they are 'obscene devices' (for example, Alabama's Anti-Obscenity Enforcement Act of 1998), while other state bans have been struck down as unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court treatment has varied: some jurisdictions upheld bans, others invalidated them on privacy grounds (invoking Lawrence v. Texas). The law differs state-by-state, and only a few states retain sex-toy sales prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: obscene vs. indecent vs. protected pornography
rubrics_metrics.description: Indecent material that is not obscene or child pornography is generally protected by the First Amendment, though the government may regulate access by minors; mere nudity alone does not render material obscene under Miller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nudity and George Carlin's 'seven dirty words' are indecent but not necessarily obscene. Jenkins v. Georgia held that occasional nudity in a film did not make it obscene. The government can use time/place/manner rules and child-protection measures to restrict indecent material without invoking obscenity law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner / zoning restrictions for sexual expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions and zoning (e.g., restrictive zoning of adult video stores; regulations on erotic dancing attire) can be used to regulate sexual expression even when obscenity convictions are difficult to obtain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts permit some indirect regulation such as zoning of adult businesses and dress rules for erotic dancers (Barnes v. Glen Theatre is cited). These are generally content-neutral or narrowly tailored restrictions rather than obscenity-based bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship in publicly funded institutions and funding conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations receiving government funding (e.g., NEA grants) may be required to abide by general decency standards as conditions on funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National Endowment for the Arts v. Finley upheld decency considerations as conditions on funding rather than direct speech regulation. Whether a venue is a 'designated public forum' matters when assessing challenges to exclusions of sexual/explicit works in public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-image/textual obscenity prosecutions and the prurient-interest requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Text-only works have been prosecuted for obscenity; courts have required proof that the work inspires or exhibits 'prurient' interest to sustain convictions (e.g., prosecutions of Fanny Hill and other texts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kaplan v. California and other cases confirm that lack of pictorial content does not immunize a book from obscenity law. The prurient-interest and 'taken as a whole' concepts apply to textual works as to visual ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms: vagueness, due process, and practical difficulties of the tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques of obscenity doctrine include difficulty defining 'obscenity', problems with 'contemporary community standards', claims that the Miller test denies defendants due process because they cannot know if material is obscene until after a jury verdict, and arguments that the prongs are incoherent (e.g., requiring the audience to be both 'turned on' and 'grossed out').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criticisms are doctrinal and policy considerations courts and commentators weigh when applying or reforming obscenity law; they explain why the law has evolved and why different jurisdictions and courts treat similar material differently.
